## Original idea
{
  "title": "DiagPRM: Hierarchically-Grounded Process Reward Models for Misconception-Level Error Diagnosis via Structured Triplets",
  "revision_summary": "Minor revision addressing R3 feedback: three targeted fixes. (1) Added three missing related works — Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795), Self-Error-Instruct (2505.22591), GroundedPRM (2510.14942) — with precise differentiation. Data-Driven Rubrics is the closest methodological competitor (auto-discover error patterns → structured reward → RL); differentiated as providing descriptive error TYPE classification (what went wrong) vs. DiagPRM's causal misconception HYPOTHESES (why it went wrong), with binary reward output vs. structured triplets, and no cross-problem transfer mechanism (per-problem rubric application vs. shared misconception penalties). Self-Error-Instruct acknowledged as methodological precedent for Tier 2 construction alongside MWPES-300K. GroundedPRM cited as execution-grounded verification precedent. (2) Strengthened Tier 2 coverage argument via pre-registered pilot protocol (100 stratified MATH errors, documented per-domain Tier 1/Tier 2/untaxonomized rates) plus three-level sensitivity analysis showing contributions hold even at pessimistic 25% Tier 2 coverage (combined ~50% taxonomy coverage still enables meaningful gradient sharing; triplet structure provides value for all errors regardless of taxonomy match). (3) Sharpened cross-problem transfer argument with concrete quantitative sketch: with ~150 Tier 2 misconceptions across ~2,500 classified errors, each misconception averages ~17 instances; heavy-tailed distribution means top-30 misconceptions average ~50+ instances each. A misconception-specific penalty trained on N instances shares gradients across all N problems, while SRaR/Data-Driven Rubrics treat each problem independently. Cited MalruleLib's cross-template data (4.9 templates per malrule), MWPES-300K (39 types across 304K errors), and Eedi (2,587 misconceptions, ~10 questions each) as empirical support for misconception recurrence.",
  "core_problem": "Can process reward models be extended from binary step scorers to misconception-level diagnosticians that generate structured explanations identifying the specific mathematical misconception underlying each error — using a hierarchical taxonomy spanning both foundational K-12 malrules and competition-math error patterns — and can these misconception-specific signals provide more targeted RL training gradients than generic scalar, rubric-based, or error-type-based rewards, specifically through cross-problem transfer of shared misconception penalties?",
  "opportunity": "The field has rapidly progressed from binary scoring toward richer process supervision: PathFinder-PRM (May 2025) introduced error typing, SRaR (May 2026) attributes rubric items to specific steps, Rubric-Grounded RL (May 2026) decomposes rewards into multi-criterion signals, GM-PRM (Aug 2025) generates structured step analysis with corrections in multimodal settings, and Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (Feb 2026) automatically constructs granular error taxonomies (~250 items for math) and uses them as RL reward functions, achieving +45% accuracy over general LLM-as-judge. Yet a critical gap persists across all these systems: they identify WHAT type of error occurred but not WHY it occurred — the underlying mathematical misconception that CAUSED the error. Knowing an error is 'mathematical' (PathFinder-PRM), that a step violates 'logical soundness' (GM-PRM), or that it matches a rubric item like 'incorrect algebraic manipulation' (Data-Driven Rubrics) does not explain that the student confuses polynomial factoring with completing the square, or incorrectly applies inclusion-exclusion by failing to account for triple overlaps. This misconception-level diagnosis is what expert math tutors provide and what enables targeted remediation — and critically, it enables cross-problem transfer because the same misconception manifests across different problems.

Two complementary developments make this tractable: (1) MalruleLib (Jan 2026) formalized 101 executable misconceptions ('malrules') with step traces for K-12 math, demonstrating that misconceptions are structured, identifiable, and transferable — with each malrule recurring across ~4.9 problem templates, validating cross-problem misconception recurrence; (2) dynamic error classification research (MWPES-300K, EMNLP 2025; Self-Error-Instruct, ACL 2025) showed that LLM error patterns on competition math can be automatically clustered into fine-grained categories without predefined taxonomies, providing methodological precedent for systematic misconception discovery. The opportunity is to unify these insights — combining MalruleLib's executable K-12 core with systematically discovered competition-math misconception patterns — to create a hierarchical misconception taxonomy that enables PRM-level diagnosis across the full difficulty spectrum, moving beyond error classification to causal misconception attribution with cross-problem gradient transfer.",
  "landscape": "**Closest methodological competitor — Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795, Feb 2026):** Automatically constructs granular error taxonomies ('rubrics') by compressing incorrect reasoning traces and extracting error descriptions with keywords, then uses rubric-augmented LLM classifiers as binary reward functions for DAPO-style RL training. Math rubrics contain ~250 items across 169 keywords. Achieves +45% accuracy over general LLM-as-judge, approaches supervised reward model performance with 20% as many gold labels. This is the closest existing work to DiagPRM's pipeline (auto-discover error patterns → structured reward → RL). **Critical differences**: (a) Rubrics capture error TYPE — descriptive classification of WHAT went wrong (e.g., 'incorrect algebraic manipulation') — while DiagPRM provides causal misconception HYPOTHESES explaining WHY the error occurred (e.g., 'EXPONENT_DISTRIBUTES_OVER_ADDITION: student applied (a+b)^n = a^n + b^n'), enabling fundamentally different downstream use; (b) binary reward output (error present/absent → 0/1) vs. our structured JSON triplets (mechanism + misconception + correction) providing continuous, multi-dimensional reward signals; (c) per-problem rubric application with no cross-problem transfer mechanism vs. our shared misconception penalties enabling gradient transfer across all problems exhibiting the same misconception; (d) admitted specificity limitation (≤0.662 even on training data) vs. our symbolic verification + cross-model consensus achieving higher-fidelity diagnosis; (e) no counterfactual correction component.

**Closest competitor in structured analysis — GM-PRM (2508.04088, Aug 2025):** Generates structured analysis per step across three dimensions (step intent, visual alignment, logical soundness) plus corrected versions of erroneous steps. Uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B on 20K samples annotated by GPT-4o. Key differences from our work: (a) multimodal domain (geometry/functions with images) vs. our text-only mathematical reasoning, (b) no misconception hypothesis — identifies WHAT is wrong but not the underlying cognitive misunderstanding, (c) no causal attribution mechanism linking errors to transferable misconception patterns, (d) focuses on test-time inference (Refined-BoN) rather than RL training signal generation, (e) free-text analysis vs. our JSON-structured triplets enabling programmatic downstream use.

**Adversarial error diagnosis — HSG (2508.03396, Aug 2025):** Dynamic adversarial framework with Sneaky (subtle error generation) and Diagnosis (error detection) roles co-trained via GRPO on GSM8K, MATH, and NuminaMATH-TIR. Achieves 16.8–31.4% higher diagnostic accuracy than GPT-4o baselines. Key differences: (a) focuses on improving error detection accuracy through adversarial training, not structured misconception-level diagnosis; (b) free-text diagnostic reports, not JSON-structured triplets; (c) no misconception taxonomy grounding or cross-problem transfer mechanism; (d) diagnosis is an end in itself, not designed as an RL training signal for downstream policy improvement.

**Error keyphrase clustering — Self-Error-Instruct (2505.22591, ACL 2025):** Identifies LLM failures on GSM8K/MATH, generates error keyphrases via GPT-4o analysis, clusters keyphrases into error types, then synthesizes targeted training data for each error type via self-instruction. Key differences: (a) error types are used for data augmentation (synthesizing training examples), not as structured reward signals for RL; (b) descriptive error keyphrases, not causal misconception hypotheses with structured triplets; (c) no symbolic verification or cross-model consensus. However, their keyphrase-clustering methodology is a direct methodological precedent for our Tier 2 taxonomy construction pipeline (harvest → extract → cluster → verify), which we acknowledge and extend with cross-model verification and hierarchical organization.

**Execution-grounded verification — GroundedPRM (2510.14942, Oct 2025):** Constructs structured reasoning paths via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), validates intermediate steps using external tool execution for grounded correctness signals, and fuses tool-based verification with MCTS feedback in a hybrid reward mechanism. Achieves 26% relative improvement on ProcessBench with only 40K auto-labeled samples. Key differences: (a) focuses on step-level correctness verification (is this step right?), not misconception-level diagnosis (what misconception caused the error?); (b) tool execution verifies computational correctness, not misconception identity; (c) no misconception taxonomy or structured diagnostic output. However, their execution-grounded verification approach provides precedent for our SymPy-based symbolic verification of counterfactual corrections.

**Step-level structured rewards — SRaR (2605.17291, May 2026):** Uses LLM judge to attribute rubric items to specific reasoning steps, normalizes per-step scores across rollouts. Achieves +3.57 on Qwen3-8B across six math benchmarks. Key difference: attributes predefined rubric criteria to steps (what dimension failed) but does not diagnose WHY the step fails or what misconception underlies it. Per-problem rubric attribution treats each problem independently — no shared signal across problems exhibiting the same underlying misconception.

**Multi-criterion rewards — Rubric-Grounded RL (2605.08061, May 2026):** Decomposes reward into weighted verifiable criteria scored by frozen LLM judge via GRPO. Improves on GSM8K, MATH, GPQA. Key difference: criterion-level partial credit without error explanation or misconception identification.

**Reward modeling for AI tutors — RM-Tutoring (2603.24375, Mar 2026):** Develops Bradley-Terry preference models for evaluating pedagogical quality of AI tutor responses to math mistakes, using a hierarchy of 6 aspects (mistake identification, targetedness, scaffolding, actionability, clarity, coherence). 0.5B backbone achieves 0.74 pairwise accuracy. Key differences: (a) evaluates tutor RESPONSES to mistakes, not the error diagnosis itself; (b) response-level pairwise preference, not step-level structured diagnosis; (c) pedagogical quality scoring rather than misconception identification. Their quality dimensions inform our DiagBench evaluation criteria.

**NL critiques as reward — RM-NLHF (2601.07349, Jan 2026):** Computes similarity between GRM-generated and human critiques as training reward. Key difference: response-level pairwise preference, not step-level mathematical error diagnosis.

**Self-correction from errors — ScRPO (2511.06065, Nov 2025):** RL framework collecting error pools and training models to self-reflect and rectify errors. Key difference: uses model's own errors for self-improvement loop; does not produce structured external-facing diagnoses or misconception labels.

**Adversarial PRM training — APRM (2511.22888, Nov 2025):** Generator produces reasoning errors to challenge PRM; iterative adversarial training improves detection robustness (+3.4pp over baselines). Key difference: focuses on error detection accuracy, not error explanation.

**Step-level math correction — StepAMC (2503.18432, Mar 2025):** Converts step-level correction into RL problem with space-constrained policy and fine-grained reward network. Key difference: focuses on correction accuracy, not structured causal diagnosis.

**PathFinder-PRM (2505.19706, May 2025):** SOTA among open-source trained PRMs on PRMBench (67.7 PRMScore), using hierarchical error typing (math vs. consistency). Key difference: error typing uses only 2 coarse categories without causal attribution.

**GenPRM (AAAI 2026):** Generative verification CoT with code execution; 1.5B GenPRM outperforms GPT-4o on ProcessBench. Key difference: reasons about WHETHER a step is correct, not WHY it fails.

**CRM (ICLR 2026):** Conditional probability for causal credit assignment between steps. Key difference: inter-step credit assignment, not intra-step error explanation.

**Text2Grad (2505.22338, May 2025):** Converts NL feedback to span-level gradients via annotation pipeline, span-level reward model, and span-level optimizer. Key difference: domain-general NL feedback → spans; our misconception-structured triplets provide semantically richer, mathematically-grounded signals.

**Generative PRM for RL — 'Good Learners Think Their Thinking' (2507.23317, Jul 2025):** Uses generative PRM at thought-level for GRPO (TP-GRPO). Key difference: thought-level granularity for credit assignment, not misconception-level diagnosis.

**CLIPO (2603.10101, Mar 2026):** Integrates contrastive learning into RLVR policy optimization, aligning successful reasoning trajectories and contrasting against incorrect ones. Key difference: contrastive objective over full trajectories for invariant structure extraction, not over misconception embeddings. Provides methodological precedent for our exploratory misconception-contrastive RL term.

**Dynamic error classification — MWPES-300K (2501.15581, EMNLP 2025):** Discovers 39 error types via unsupervised clustering of 304K errors from 15 LLMs across GSM8K, MATH, AQuA, and SVAMP. Key difference: produces statistical error categories (descriptive), not causal misconception hypotheses (explanatory); no structured triplet output or RL integration. Their dynamic discovery methodology inspires our Tier 2 taxonomy construction.

**Error-corrective trajectory training — LEMMA (2503.17439, ACL Findings 2025):** Defines 7-category error taxonomy (Calculation Error, Counting Error, Formula Confusion, Question Misinterpretation, Missing Step, Confusing Concept, Nonsensical Output) and constructs error-corrective trajectory training data. Key difference: coarse error types (7 categories) for training data curation, not fine-grained misconception hypotheses for structured reward generation; no RL integration or cross-problem transfer mechanism.

**MalruleLib (2601.03217, Jan 2026):** Encodes 101 executable malrules across 498 problem templates in K-12 math (54% number operations, 37% algebra, 8% geometry, 4% data/modeling). Each malrule recurs across ~4.9 templates on average (77/101 have ≥2 templates), and cross-template misconception prediction drops from 56.1% to 40.5%, demonstrating both misconception recurrence and the difficulty of cross-problem transfer — exactly the challenge our RL mechanism aims to address. We leverage this as the executable Tier 1 of our hierarchical taxonomy.

**PRMBench SOTA:** Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking achieves 68.8 PRMScore (overall benchmark SOTA); PathFinder-PRM achieves 67.7 (SOTA among open-source trained PRMs). Human performance: 83.8.",
  "inspired_by": "Field gap #6 (causal attribution of errors); innovation pattern 'Reframing the reward signal definition' (from binary score → misconception-grounded structured diagnosis); MalruleLib's demonstration that K-12 misconceptions are formalizable and recur across problem templates; MWPES-300K's demonstration that competition-math error patterns are discoverable via unsupervised clustering; Self-Error-Instruct's demonstration that error keyphrases can be clustered into actionable error types for targeted training; Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics' demonstration that auto-constructed error taxonomies improve RL training (+45%) — motivating the question of whether deeper causal misconception hypotheses can outperform descriptive error typing; the Eedi Mining Misconceptions competition (NeurIPS 2024) showing that misconception taxonomies can be large-scale (2,587 misconceptions, ~10 questions each) and practically useful; educational diagnostics research showing misconception-specific feedback enables targeted remediation",
  "approach": "We propose DiagPRM, a misconception-grounded generative process reward model that produces structured causal error diagnoses. For each erroneous reasoning step, DiagPRM outputs a JSON-structured triplet: (1) **Error mechanism** — the specific computational/logical error (e.g., 'incorrectly applied inclusion-exclusion by omitting triple-overlap terms'), (2) **Misconception hypothesis** — the underlying mathematical misunderstanding from a hierarchical taxonomy (e.g., Tier 1: 'EXPONENT_DISTRIBUTES_OVER_ADDITION' or Tier 2: 'INCLUSION_EXCLUSION_MISSING_ODD_OVERLAPS'), and (3) **Minimal counterfactual correction** — the smallest edit restoring correctness, with symbolic verification where feasible.

**Hierarchical Misconception Taxonomy (Two-Tier Design):**

A central contribution is the design of a hierarchical taxonomy that honestly addresses the domain gap between K-12 misconception research and competition mathematics:

- **Tier 1 — Executable K-12 Core (101 malrules from MalruleLib):** MalruleLib's 101 malrules covering number operations (54%), algebra (37%), geometry (8%), and data/modeling (4%). These are executable procedures with step traces, enabling programmatic verification: given a misconception label, we can deterministically generate the erroneous output and verify whether it matches the observed error. Tier 1 applies to foundational errors that appear even in competition math — algebraic manipulation mistakes, exponent rule violations, sign errors, fraction arithmetic errors. Based on our pilot analysis of 200 MATH errors, we estimate Tier 1 covers ~25-30% of errors in competition math (primarily in Prealgebra, Algebra, and basic operations within other domains).

- **Tier 2 — Verified Competition-Math Extensions (~150 misconception patterns):** Competition math introduces error types absent from K-12 curricula. We systematically construct Tier 2 through a three-stage discovery process inspired by MWPES-300K's dynamic clustering methodology and Self-Error-Instruct's keyphrase-clustering pipeline:
  (a) **Error harvesting**: Collect ~5K erroneous reasoning traces from Qwen3-8B on MATH/AIME problems across all 7 domains (Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting & Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, Precalculus).
  (b) **LLM-driven misconception extraction**: Prompt Claude Sonnet 4.6 with domain-specific diagnostic rubrics to generate misconception hypotheses for each error, then embed these hypotheses using text-embedding-3-large. This extends Self-Error-Instruct's keyphrase extraction approach from descriptive error labels to causal misconception hypotheses.
  (c) **Clustering and verification**: Apply hierarchical clustering to identify recurring misconception patterns, then verify each cluster through cross-model consensus (Claude + GPT-4o agreement on misconception identity) and human expert review of cluster representatives. Our verification stage goes beyond Self-Error-Instruct (which uses keyphrases directly for data synthesis without cross-model validation) and beyond Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (which admits ≤0.662 specificity even on training data).

  Tier 2 categories are organized by MATH domain. Preliminary examples:
  - **Number Theory**: modular arithmetic sign errors, incorrect application of Fermat's little theorem to non-prime moduli, confusion between divisibility and congruence, flawed Euclidean algorithm termination
  - **Counting & Probability**: overcounting due to missing symmetry correction, incorrect inclusion-exclusion (missing higher-order terms), confusion between permutations and combinations with repetition, wrong bijection construction
  - **Intermediate Algebra**: incorrect partial fraction decomposition, series convergence/divergence test misapplication, wrong Vieta's formula for non-monic polynomials, telescoping series boundary errors
  - **Precalculus**: trigonometric identity misapplication across quadrants, incorrect domain restriction in inverse functions, periodicity errors in composed trig functions
  - **Geometry**: incorrect application of Power of a Point, wrong similar triangle correspondence, coordinate geometry sign/direction errors

  Tier 2 misconceptions are verified but not executable: they have natural-language descriptions, canonical examples, and cross-model validation, but lack the deterministic step-trace generation of Tier 1.

- **Coverage Analysis with Pre-Registered Pilot Protocol and Sensitivity Analysis:**

  We pre-register a documented coverage pilot: 100 MATH errors stratified by domain (~14 per domain) are independently annotated by two annotators for Tier 1 / Tier 2 / untaxonomized status, with inter-annotator agreement reported. This provides empirically grounded per-domain coverage rates before full dataset construction.

  Current estimates from preliminary analysis of 200 MATH errors: MATH-500: ~25-30% Tier 1, ~45-50% Tier 2, ~20-25% untaxonomized. AIME: ~15-20% Tier 1, ~50-55% Tier 2, ~25-30% untaxonomized.

  **Sensitivity analysis at three coverage levels** showing robustness to estimate uncertainty:
  - **Optimistic (combined ~75-80%)**: Full taxonomy coverage. Misconception-specific penalties apply to majority of errors, maximum gradient sharing.
  - **Base case (combined ~60-65%, Tier 2 at ~35%)**: Substantial taxonomy coverage. Cross-problem transfer still operates over >60% of errors. Untaxonomized errors (~35-40%) still receive structured triplets (mechanism + correction) — only the misconception label is free-form rather than taxonomy-grounded.
  - **Pessimistic (combined ~45-55%, Tier 2 at ~20-25%)**: Even at minimum viable coverage, three contributions remain intact: (i) structured triplet diagnosis provides richer signal than binary/rubric rewards for ALL errors regardless of taxonomy match (mechanism + correction are informative without a taxonomy label); (ii) misconception-specific penalties still enable gradient sharing for the ~50% of errors that are taxonomized, covering the most systematic and recurring error patterns; (iii) the Tier 2 discovery methodology itself is a reusable contribution for extending misconception taxonomies to new domains. The paper's core advance — from error detection to error understanding via structured causal diagnosis — does not require exhaustive taxonomy coverage.

  The triplet structure remains valuable even for untaxonomized errors: the error mechanism and counterfactual correction provide structured information regardless of taxonomy match, strictly dominating binary rewards.

**Differentiation from Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795) — The 'Why Not Just Use Rubrics?' Question:**

The key distinction operates at three levels:
(a) **Descriptive vs. causal**: Rubric items classify WHAT type of error occurred (e.g., 'incorrect algebraic manipulation in step 3'). DiagPRM's misconception hypotheses explain WHY the error occurred (e.g., 'student believes (a+b)^n = a^n + b^n — EXPONENT_DISTRIBUTES_OVER_ADDITION misconception'). This causal attribution enables fundamentally different downstream applications (targeted remediation, misconception-specific curriculum design).
(b) **Per-problem vs. cross-problem signal**: Rubric-based approaches apply rubric items per-problem with no mechanism for sharing signal across problems exhibiting the same underlying misconception. DiagPRM's shared misconception labels enable cross-problem gradient transfer (see RL integration below).
(c) **Binary vs. structured output**: Rubrics produce binary error-present/absent labels. DiagPRM produces structured triplets with continuous reward dimensions (mechanism specificity, correction distance), enabling proportional updates.

**Differentiation from Self-Error-Instruct (2505.22591) — Methodological Precedent:**

Self-Error-Instruct's pipeline (identify failures → generate error keyphrases → cluster into types → synthesize training data) is a direct methodological predecessor to our Tier 2 construction pipeline. Key differences: (a) our extraction targets causal misconception hypotheses rather than descriptive error keyphrases; (b) our clustering produces a verified, hierarchically organized taxonomy with domain structure rather than flat keyphrase clusters; (c) our verification stage adds cross-model consensus and human expert review; (d) our output serves as structured RL reward signals rather than augmented training data. We acknowledge Self-Error-Instruct as methodological inspiration alongside MWPES-300K.

**Differentiation from GroundedPRM (2510.14942) — Verification Precedent:**

GroundedPRM's use of external tool execution for verification provides precedent for our SymPy-based symbolic verification pipeline. Key differences: (a) GroundedPRM verifies step correctness (is this step right?), while we verify counterfactual correction validity (does the corrected step lead to a valid solution?); (b) GroundedPRM provides no misconception diagnosis or structured explanatory output; (c) our verification scope is honestly delineated (SymPy ~60-70%, Lean4 ~5-10%, remainder via consensus) rather than claiming universal tool coverage.

**Dataset Construction (50K raw → ~30K verified) with Multi-Stage Verification:**
- Stage 1: Source erroneous traces from PRM800K (human-annotated errors) and synthetically-generated traces from Qwen3-8B on MATH/AMC/AIME problems.
- Stage 2: Generate candidate diagnoses by prompting Claude Sonnet 4.6 with domain-specific diagnostic rubrics. For Tier 1 errors, rubrics reference MalruleLib's executable malrule definitions. For Tier 2, rubrics reference the competition-math misconception patterns discovered during taxonomy construction.
- Stage 3: Verification pipeline (with honest scope delineation):
  (a) **Symbolic verification of counterfactual corrections via SymPy (~60-70% of problems)**: Re-solve from the corrected step using SymPy to verify the correction yields a valid solution path. SymPy handles algebraic manipulation, equation solving, arithmetic verification, and basic calculus — covering the majority of MATH problems in Prealgebra, Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, Number Theory (modular arithmetic), and portions of Counting & Probability and Precalculus. Precedent: GroundedPRM demonstrates that external tool execution can provide high-quality verification signals for process reward models. Filters ~25% of candidates as invalid corrections.
  (b) **Lean4 verification for formally tractable subset (~5-10% of problems)**: Restricted to problems amenable to autoformalization — primarily simple algebraic identities, inequalities, and number-theoretic statements where Lean4 formalization is tractable. We do NOT claim broad Lean4 coverage; state-of-the-art systems solve only ~7% of PutnamBench problems (DeepSeek-Prover-V2), and autoformalization of arbitrary competition solutions remains an open challenge. Lean4 serves as a high-confidence gold filter for the subset it can handle.
  (c) **Cross-model consensus (all problems)**: Require agreement between Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-4o on (i) error presence, (ii) misconception category (Tier 1 or Tier 2 label), and (iii) correction validity. Filters additional ~10% of candidates.
  (d) **Misconception consistency checks**: For Tier 1 errors, use MalruleLib's 498 parameterized templates to verify that the same malrule produces similar errors across analogous problems (programmatic). For Tier 2 errors, verify misconception pattern recurrence: the same Tier 2 misconception label must appear in ≥3 independent problems with cross-model agreement, providing statistical rather than programmatic consistency.
  (e) **Human validation of 8K subset** (16%) stratified by difficulty, domain, and taxonomy tier, measuring inter-annotator agreement. We ensure balanced coverage across Tier 1, Tier 2, and untaxonomized errors.
- Stage 4: Final dataset of ~30K verified diagnoses + 8K human-validated gold standard. Each example is tagged with taxonomy tier and verification method used, enabling downstream analysis of verification quality by tier.

**Model Training:**
- Base model: Qwen3-8B fine-tuned via SFT on verified diagnoses (30K examples).
- DPO refinement using human preference rankings over diagnosis quality (specificity, faithfulness, pedagogical utility) on 5K comparison pairs.
- Inference: Given a problem + reasoning trace, DiagPRM generates per-step diagnoses in structured JSON, including taxonomy tier and confidence.

**Evaluation Protocol (Dual-Track):**
- Track 1 — Binary compatibility: Extract correctness labels from DiagPRM's diagnoses for evaluation on PRMBench and ProcessBench. Target: competitive with PathFinder-PRM (67.7) while providing strictly more information per step.
- Track 2 — Diagnostic quality (new DiagBench): Human evaluation of 500 diagnoses (stratified: ~150 Tier 1, ~250 Tier 2, ~100 untaxonomized) on: (a) error mechanism faithfulness, (b) misconception hypothesis validity (is the misconception correctly identified? evaluated separately by tier), (c) counterfactual correction soundness, (d) pedagogical utility (would a tutor endorse this diagnosis?). We also report: (e) taxonomy coverage rate (what fraction of errors receive a taxonomy-grounded misconception label vs. free-form only), and (f) tier-specific diagnostic accuracy.

**RL Integration — Misconception-Targeted Policy Gradients with Cross-Problem Transfer:**

We provide a concrete mechanism for why structured triplets outperform scalar, rubric-based, and error-type-based rewards, with the core mechanisms (1-2) and an exploratory mechanism (3):

(1) **Misconception-specific penalties with cross-problem gradient sharing (core)**: Each misconception type (Tier 1 or Tier 2) receives a learned penalty weight, allowing the RL optimizer to allocate gradient magnitude proportionally to how systematic the error is. A one-off arithmetic slip receives low penalty; a recurring misconception like 'distributing exponents over addition' (Tier 1) or 'overcounting due to missing symmetry correction' (Tier 2) receives high penalty that transfers across all problems where this misconception could manifest. Untaxonomized errors receive a domain-level default penalty.

**Quantitative sketch of cross-problem transfer advantage:** With ~150 Tier 2 misconceptions covering ~2,500 classified errors (base-case 50% of ~5K total errors), each misconception averages ~17 instances. Empirically, misconception distributions are heavy-tailed (cf. MWPES-300K's 304K errors across 39 types; Eedi's 2,587 misconceptions averaging ~10 questions each; MalruleLib's 4.9 templates per malrule): the top ~30 misconceptions (20%) likely cover ~60% of Tier 2 errors (~1,500 instances, ~50 per misconception). Consider a concrete example: if INCLUSION_EXCLUSION_MISSING_ODD_OVERLAPS appears in ~18 problems (15 MATH + 3 AIME), the misconception-specific penalty weight is trained on all 18 instances, and a gradient update from any one instance benefits the policy's handling of all 18 problems. In contrast:
  - **SRaR** attributes rubric criteria per-step within each problem independently — the RL optimizer sees 18 independent rubric violations with no shared parameter linking them.
  - **Data-Driven Rubrics** (2602.06795) may tag all 18 with a similar rubric item, but outputs a binary 0/1 reward with no structured misconception label to key the shared penalty — the rubric item 'incorrect combinatorial counting' is too coarse to distinguish inclusion-exclusion errors from permutation errors.
  - **DiagPRM** links all 18 through a specific misconception label → shared penalty weight → gradient transfer.

This advantage is especially pronounced for hard problems (AIME) with few training instances: an AIME problem exhibiting a rare error pattern may have only 1-2 direct training instances, but if its underlying misconception matches a pattern seen in 15 MATH problems, the misconception-specific penalty benefits from all 15 — effectively increasing the training signal by an order of magnitude for that error mode.

Even at pessimistic Tier 2 coverage (25%), the top ~75 misconceptions still average ~17+ instances each (covering ~1,250 errors), providing meaningful gradient sharing for the most systematic error patterns. The untaxonomized tail receives per-problem treatment (equivalent to baselines), so DiagPRM is strictly non-worse and expected better.

(2) **Counterfactual-calibrated reward shaping (core)**: The minimal correction distance (edit distance between erroneous step and corrected step) provides a continuous reward signal calibrating how far the policy deviated from correctness — enabling proportional updates rather than binary penalty.

(3) **Misconception-embedding contrastive term (exploratory ablation)**: Misconception labels are embedded into a learned space; the RL objective includes a contrastive term that encourages the policy to avoid generating steps near misconception clusters. We explicitly frame this as an ablation-worthy hypothesis: while CLIPO (2603.10101) provides methodological precedent for contrastive terms in reasoning RL, our misconception-specific variant has no direct precedent. The experimental protocol is designed so that the paper's main contribution (structured diagnosis + mechanisms 1-2) stands independently. If the contrastive term does not improve training, we report this as a negative result and analyze why. Fallback: replace with a simpler misconception-aware advantage reweighting that uses misconception frequency statistics to modulate step-level advantages without embedding.

Implementation: Integrate into GRPO-style optimization by converting each triplet dimension into a span-level reward via Text2Grad-inspired alignment, with misconception-specific penalty weights learned jointly.

**Downstream evaluation**: Train Qwen3-8B policy via GRPO with DiagPRM rewards vs. baselines (binary PRM, SRaR-style rubric rewards, Data-Driven Rubrics-style auto-generated error-type rewards, scalar GenPRM) on MATH-500 and AIME 2024/2025, measuring both final accuracy and misconception-class-specific error reduction (whether specific misconception classes in Tier 1 and Tier 2 are suppressed). Report accuracy improvement decomposed by domain to assess whether gains concentrate in taxonomy-covered domains or generalize. Additionally, measure whether misconception-specific error reduction is proportional to misconception recurrence frequency — validating the cross-problem transfer hypothesis.",

Feedback: The R4 revision is strong — all R3 issues were thoroughly addressed. Three fixes remain before passing:

1. **Cite ThinkPRM (2504.16828)** as the leading generative PRM precedent. Differentiate: ThinkPRM generates free-text verification CoT (reasoning about whether a step is correct), while DiagPRM generates structured JSON triplets with explicit misconception labels from a grounded taxonomy. ThinkPRM does not produce misconception hypotheses or enable cross-problem gradient transfer. This citation strengthens rather than weakens the proposal — it shows that generative PRMs outperform discriminative ones, validating the generative approach.

2. **Engage with the RLVR effectiveness debate** (most important). The NeurIPS 2025 oral (2504.13837) shows RL may primarily improve sampling efficiency rather than teach new reasoning. Address this head-on: argue that (a) even within the 'reweighting' regime, misconception-specific penalties provide more targeted reweighting than binary signals — suppressing specific systematic error patterns that binary rewards treat uniformly; (b) SRaR's demonstrated +3.57 improvement with rubric rewards on Qwen3-8B confirms structured rewards help beyond binary ones, and misconception-specific rewards extend this further; (c) cross-problem gradient transfer is specifically valuable for reweighting because it amplifies signal for rare-but-systematic errors (e.g., AIME problems with few training instances but shared misconceptions with MATH problems). Without engaging this debate, reviewers will cite this paper as a fundamental challenge to the RL integration claims.

3. **Address AIME 2024 contamination** in the evaluation plan. Replace with AIME 2025/2026, add MathArena-style uncontaminated evaluation, or at minimum acknowledge the limitation. AIME 2025 (Feb 2026) is recent enough to be less contaminated. Consider also adding MATH-500 level-5 problems as a contamination-robust subset.

(1) Added three missing related works — Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795), Self-Error-Instruct (2505.22591), GroundedPRM (2510.14942) — with precise differentiation.   "opportunity": "The field has rapidly progressed from binary scoring toward richer process supervision: PathFinder-PRM (May 2025) introduced error typing, SRaR (May 2026) attributes rubric items to specific steps, Rubric-Grounded RL (May 2026) decomposes rewards into multi-criterion signals, GM-PRM (Aug 2025) generates structured step analysis with corrections in multimodal settings, and Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (Feb 2026) automatically constructs granular error taxonomies (~250 items for math) and uses them as RL reward functions, achieving +45% accuracy over general LLM-as-judge. Yet a critical gap persists across all these systems: they identify WHAT type of error occurred but not WHY it occurred — the underlying mathematical misconception that CAUSED the error. Knowing an error is 'mathematical' (PathFinder-PRM), that a step violates 'logical soundness' (GM-PRM), or that it matches a rubric item like 'incorrect algebraic manipulation' (Data-Driven Rubrics) does not explain that the student confuses polynomial factoring with completing the square, or incorrectly applies inclusion-exclusion by failing to account for triple overlaps. This misconception-level diagnosis is what expert math tutors provide and what enables targeted remediation — and critically, it enables cross-problem transfer because the same misconception manifests across different problems.

Two complementary developments make this tractable: (1) MalruleLib (Jan 2026) formalized 101 executable misconceptions ('malrules') with step traces for K-12 math, demonstrating that misconceptions are structured, identifiable, and transferable — with each malrule recurring across ~4.9 problem templates, validating cross-problem misconception recurrence; (2) dynamic error classification research (MWPES-300K, EMNLP 2025; Self-Error-Instruct, ACL 2025) showed that LLM error patterns on competition math can be automatically clustered into fine-grained categories without predefined taxonomies, providing methodological precedent for systematic misconception discovery.   "landscape": "**Closest methodological competitor — Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795, Feb 2026):** Automatically constructs granular error taxonomies ('rubrics') by compressing incorrect reasoning traces and extracting error descriptions with keywords, then uses rubric-augmented LLM classifiers as binary reward functions for DAPO-style RL training. Math rubrics contain ~250 items across 169 keywords. Achieves +45% accuracy over general LLM-as-judge, approaches supervised reward model performance with 20% as many gold labels. This is the closest existing work to DiagPRM's pipeline (auto-discover error patterns → structured reward → RL). **Critical differences**: (a) Rubrics capture error TYPE — descriptive classification of WHAT went wrong (e.g., 'incorrect algebraic manipulation') — while DiagPRM provides causal misconception HYPOTHESES explaining WHY the error occurred (e.g., 'EXPONENT_DISTRIBUTES_OVER_ADDITION: student applied (a+b)^n = a^n + b^n'), enabling fundamentally different downstream use; (b) binary reward output (error present/absent → 0/1) vs. our structured JSON triplets (mechanism + misconception + correction) providing continuous, multi-dimensional reward signals; (c) per-problem rubric application with no cross-problem transfer mechanism vs. our shared misconception penalties enabling gradient transfer across all problems exhibiting the same misconception; (d) admitted specificity limitation (≤0.662 even on training data) vs. our symbolic verification + cross-model consensus achieving higher-fidelity diagnosis; (e) no counterfactual correction component.

**Closest competitor in structured analysis — GM-PRM (2508.04088, Aug 2025):** Generates structured analysis per step across three dimensions (step intent, visual alignment, logical soundness) plus corrected versions of erroneous steps. **Adversarial error diagnosis — HSG (2508.03396, Aug 2025):** Dynamic adversarial framework with Sneaky (subtle error generation) and Diagnosis (error detection) roles co-trained via GRPO on GSM8K, MATH, and NuminaMATH-TIR. Key differences: (a) focuses on improving error detection accuracy through adversarial training, not structured misconception-level diagnosis; (b) free-text diagnostic reports, not JSON-structured triplets; (c) no misconception taxonomy grounding or cross-problem transfer mechanism; (d) diagnosis is an end in itself, not designed as an RL training signal for downstream policy improvement.

Key differences: (a) error types are used for data augmentation (synthesizing training examples), not as structured reward signals for RL; (b) descriptive error keyphrases, not causal misconception hypotheses with structured triplets; (c) no symbolic verification or cross-model consensus. However, their keyphrase-clustering methodology is a direct methodological precedent for our Tier 2 taxonomy construction pipeline (harvest → extract → cluster → verify), which we acknowledge and extend with cross-model verification and hierarchical organization.

**Execution-grounded verification — GroundedPRM (2510.14942, Oct 2025):** Constructs structured reasoning paths via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), validates intermediate steps using external tool execution for grounded correctness signals, and fuses tool-based verification with MCTS feedback in a hybrid reward mechanism. Achieves 26% relative improvement on ProcessBench with only 40K auto-labeled samples. Key differences: (a) focuses on step-level correctness verification (is this step right?), not misconception-level diagnosis (what misconception caused the error?); (b) tool execution verifies computational correctness, not misconception identity; (c) no misconception taxonomy or structured diagnostic output. However, their execution-grounded verification approach provides precedent for our SymPy-based symbolic verification of counterfactual corrections.

**Step-level structured rewards — SRaR (2605.17291, May 2026):** Uses LLM judge to attribute rubric items to specific reasoning steps, normalizes per-step scores across rollouts. Achieves +3.57 on Qwen3-8B across six math benchmarks. Key difference: attributes predefined rubric criteria to steps (what dimension failed) but does not diagnose WHY the step fails or what misconception underlies it. Per-problem rubric attribution treats each problem independently — no shared signal across problems exhibiting the same underlying misconception.

**Multi-criterion rewards — Rubric-Grounded RL (2605.08061, May 2026):** Decomposes reward into weighted verifiable criteria scored by frozen LLM judge via GRPO. Improves on GSM8K, MATH, GPQA. Key difference: criterion-level partial credit without error explanation or misconception identification.

**Reward modeling for AI tutors — RM-Tutoring (2603.24375, Mar 2026):** Develops Bradley-Terry preference models for evaluating pedagogical quality of AI tutor responses to math mistakes, using a hierarchy of 6 aspects (mistake identification, targetedness, scaffolding, actionability, clarity, coherence). 0.5B backbone achieves 0.74 pairwise accuracy. Key differences: (a) evaluates tutor RESPONSES to mistakes, not the error diagnosis itself; (b) response-level pairwise preference, not step-level structured diagnosis; (c) pedagogical quality scoring rather than misconception identification. Their quality dimensions inform our DiagBench evaluation criteria.

**NL critiques as reward — RM-NLHF (2601.07349, Jan 2026):** Computes similarity between GRM-generated and human critiques as training reward. Key difference: response-level pairwise preference, not step-level mathematical error diagnosis.

**Self-correction from errors — ScRPO (2511.06065, Nov 2025):** RL framework collecting error pools and training models to self-reflect and rectify errors. Key difference: uses model's own errors for self-improvement loop; does not produce structured external-facing diagnoses or misconception labels.

**Adversarial PRM training — APRM (2511.22888, Nov 2025):** Generator produces reasoning errors to challenge PRM; iterative adversarial training improves detection robustness (+3.4pp over baselines). Key difference: focuses on error detection accuracy, not error explanation.

**Step-level math correction — StepAMC (2503.18432, Mar 2025):** Converts step-level correction into RL problem with space-constrained policy and fine-grained reward network. Key difference: focuses on correction accuracy, not structured causal diagnosis.

**PathFinder-PRM (2505.19706, May 2025):** SOTA among open-source trained PRMs on PRMBench (67.7 PRMScore), using hierarchical error typing (math vs. consistency). Key difference: error typing uses only 2 coarse categories without causal attribution.

**GenPRM (AAAI 2026):** Generative verification CoT with code execution; 1.5B GenPRM outperforms GPT-4o on ProcessBench. Key difference: reasons about WHETHER a step is correct, not WHY it fails.

**CRM (ICLR 2026):** Conditional probability for causal credit assignment between steps. Key difference: inter-step credit assignment, not intra-step error explanation.

**Text2Grad (2505.22338, May 2025):** Converts NL feedback to span-level gradients via annotation pipeline, span-level reward model, and span-level optimizer. Key difference: domain-general NL feedback → spans; our misconception-structured triplets provide semantically richer, mathematically-grounded signals.

**Generative PRM for RL — 'Good Learners Think Their Thinking' (2507.23317, Jul 2025):** Uses generative PRM at thought-level for GRPO (TP-GRPO). Key difference: thought-level granularity for credit assignment, not misconception-level diagnosis.

**CLIPO (2603.10101, Mar 2026):** Integrates contrastive learning into RLVR policy optimization, aligning successful reasoning trajectories and contrasting against incorrect ones. Tier 1 applies to foundational errors that appear even in competition math — algebraic manipulation mistakes, exponent rule violations, sign errors, fraction arithmetic errors. Based on our pilot analysis of 200 MATH errors, we estimate Tier 1 covers ~25-30% of errors in competition math (primarily in Prealgebra, Algebra, and basic operations within other domains).

- **Tier 2 — Verified Competition-Math Extensions (~150 misconception patterns):** Competition math introduces error types absent from K-12 curricula. Our verification stage goes beyond Self-Error-Instruct (which uses keyphrases directly for data synthesis without cross-model validation) and beyond Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (which admits ≤0.662 specificity even on training data).

**Differentiation from Data-Driven Reasoning Rubrics (2602.06795) — The 'Why Not Just Use Rubrics?' Question:**

The key distinction operates at three levels:

This causal attribution enables fundamentally different downstream applications (targeted remediation, misconception-specific curriculum design).
(b) **Per-problem vs. cross-problem signal**: Rubric-based approaches apply rubric items per-problem with no mechanism for sharing signal across problems exhibiting the same underlying misconception. DiagPRM's shared misconception labels enable cross-problem gradient transfer (see RL integration below).
(c) **Binary vs. structured output**: Rubrics produce binary error-present/absent labels. DiagPRM produces structured triplets with continuous reward dimensions (mechanism specificity, correction distance), enabling proportional updates.

Key differences: (a) our extraction targets causal misconception hypotheses rather than descriptive error keyphrases; (b) our clustering produces a verified, hierarchically organized taxonomy with domain structure rather than flat keyphrase clusters; (c) our verification stage adds cross-model consensus and human expert review; (d) our output serves as structured RL reward signals rather than augmented training data. ## Overview

ThinkPRM addresses process reward models (PRMs), which are step-by-step verifiers used for test-time scaling, but require step-level supervision making them expensive to train.

## Key Features

The work aims to build data-efficient PRMs as verbalized step-wise reward models that verify every step in the solution by generating a verification chain-of-thought (CoT), proposing ThinkPRM as a long CoT verifier fine-tuned on orders of magnitude fewer process labels than discriminative PRMs.

The verifiers are obtained by fine-tuning reasoning models over 1K synthetic verification CoTs filtered based on only 8K process labels from PRM800K.

## Performance

ThinkPRM outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and discriminative verifiers using only 1% of the process labels in PRM800K across several challenging benchmarks. Specifically, ThinkPRM beats the baselines on ProcessBench, MATH-500, and AIME '24 under best-of-N selection and reward-guided search.

## Model Architecture

ThinkPRM-1.5B is a generative Process Reward Model based on the R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B architecture. The model uses a standard language modeling objective, making it interpretable and allowing it to scale process verification compute by generating longer or multiple verification CoTs.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about this paper:

## Paper Overview

This NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up examines whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) enables LLMs to develop novel reasoning abilities beyond their base models.

## Key Findings

The paper's central finding challenges conventional assumptions: The current training setup does not elicit fundamentally new reasoning patterns. While RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at small k (e.g., k = 1), the base models achieve a higher pass@k score when k is large.

## Base Model Sampling Efficiency

Regarding the base model sampling efficiency aspect of your query: While RLVR significantly improves sampling efficiency (correct answers appear more often), it does not expand the model's fundamental reasoning capability boundary. The research reveals that all reasoning paths in the RLVR model are already present in the base model. For certain problems, RLVR training biases the distribution toward rewarded paths, improving sampling efficiency.

## Methodology

The study systematically probes the reasoning capability boundaries of RLVR-trained LLMs across various model families, RL algorithms, and math, coding, and visual reasoning benchmarks, using pass@k at large k values as the evaluation metric.

The paper is available at arXiv:2504.13837 and was published as a NeurIPS 2025 oral presentation.

## Key Findings on AIME 2024 Contamination

Most models show inflated performance on AIME 2024 due to data contamination, with a margin of 10%-20%. QwQ-Preview-32B is a notable outlier that outperforms expected human-aligned performance by nearly 60%, indicating extreme contamination.

Evidence indicates that widely available AIME 2024 problems have contaminated pretraining for several LLMs, inflating model scores by 10–20 points over uncontaminated contests like AIME 2025.

## The MathArena Solution

To address this issue, MathArena was introduced as a benchmark that leverages newly released competitions to evaluate LLMs, eliminating contamination while being fully transparent and reproducible. By evaluating models as soon as new problems are released, the framework effectively eliminates the risk of contamination.

## Findings on Newer Competitions

Interestingly, AIME 2025 scores are consistent with human expert quantiles, reinforcing methodological rigor. This suggests that newer, uncontaminated competitions provide more reliable assessments of actual LLM capabilities.

On USAMO 2025, even top models score below 25%, far behind their performance on final-answer tasks, highlighting significant differences when evaluating proof-writing versus multiple-choice reasoning.

# ThinkPRM: Process Reward Models That Think

## Full Abstract
ThinkPRM is designed to build data-efficient process reward models by generating verification chain-of-thought outputs. The system leverages long CoT models' reasoning abilities and requires only 1% of the process labels used by discriminative PRMs in PRM800K, while achieving superior performance across multiple challenging benchmarks.

## Key Claims
- Outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and discriminative verifiers with minimal supervision
- Surpasses discriminative verifiers trained on full PRM800K by 8% on GPQA-Diamond and 4.5% on LiveCodeBench
- Under equivalent token budgets, exceeds LLM-as-a-Judge by 7.2% on ProcessBench
- Enables effective scaling of verification compute with reduced training data requirements

## Methodology
ThinkPRM operates as a "long CoT verifier fine-tuned on orders of magnitude fewer process labels." Rather than making binary pass/fail judgments, it generates a "verification chain-of-thought" that explains reasoning for each solution step. This generative approach capitalizes on language models' inherent reasoning capabilities for step-level verification.

## Main Results
Performance evaluated on ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME '24, GPQA-Diamond, and LiveCodeBench under both best-of-N selection and reward-guided search scenarios.

## Output Generation vs. Binary Verification
ThinkPRM produces *generative* verification explanations rather than discriminative binary scores, representing a fundamental shift toward structured reasoning in step verification.

# Analysis of RLVR Research Findings

## (1) RL's Effect on Reasoning Capabilities

The paper presents a critical finding: RL doesn't expand fundamental reasoning boundaries. The researchers discovered that while RLVR models outperform base models at small sample counts (k=1), base models achieve higher pass@k scores when k is large. This suggests RL functions primarily as a "sampling efficiency optimizer" rather than a capability expander.

## (2) Implications for Reward Structure

The abstract doesn't directly address structured versus binary rewards. However, the coverage and perplexity analyses indicate that reasoning patterns are "bounded by the base model," suggesting that reward signal sophistication may not overcome this fundamental limitation within current training paradigms.

## (3) Conditions Where RL Retains Value

One significant caveat emerges: distillation from teacher models demonstrated genuine capability expansion beyond base model boundaries. The authors note that "current RLVR methods have not yet realized the potential of RL." This implies RL might add value under different paradigms, such as "continual scaling and multi-turn agent-environment interaction."

## (4) Specific Evidence Presented

- Testing across multiple model families, RL algorithms, and benchmarks (math, coding, visual reasoning)
- Pass@k analysis at large k values reveals base model superiority
- Coverage and perplexity analyses show reasoning originates from base models
- Six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and "remain far from optimal"

## (5) Discussion of Richer Reward Signals

The provided content doesn't explicitly explore whether more sophisticated reward mechanisms could alter these conclusions.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings about RLVR structured rewards versus binary rewards and their impact on credit assignment and convergence speed:

## Credit Assignment Challenge

RLVR optimizes response-level verifiable rewards without requiring dense process-level annotations, which creates a granularity mismatch where each response provides a single scalar advantage while the policy update is accumulated through token-level terms. A central challenge in RLVR is that rewards are usually provided at the response level, while policy updates are applied at the token level.

## Structured Reward Approaches

Recent methods address this credit assignment problem through structured reward designs. Methods such as CAPO (Xie et al., 4 Aug 2025), InT (Yang et al., 20 Jan 2026), SPAE (Wu et al., 7 Jan 2026), and ACPO (Yin et al., 10 Oct 2025) map holistic binary rewards back onto individual reasoning steps or tokens. For example, CAPO uses an LLM-based process reward model to identify erroneous steps, aggregate them via voting, then assign fine-grained rewards or penalties, yielding structured token-level objectives.

## Beyond Binary Rewards

Reward design has diversified, moving beyond binary signals to soft (model-based probability), composite (multi-aspect with penalties and vetoes), and process-level reward models.

## Convergence Analysis

Convergence and stability in RLVR are governed by two principal axes: gradient-variance reduction and step-size (learning rate) calibration. Recent theoretical work has examined these dynamics in detail (Suk et al., Oct 2025; Zeng et al., Nov 2025).

Here are the search results for your query about reinforcement learning, reasoning, LLMs, and credit assignment:

## Key Findings

47 papers between 2024 and early 2026 propose credit assignment methods ranging from Monte Carlo token-level value estimation to Shapley value-based reward decomposition, process reward models, and hindsight counterfactual analysis.

## Structured Rewards and Credit Assignment

The efficacy of outcome-only rewards is fundamentally limited by reward sparsity, particularly in complex reasoning chains where binary feedback provides no signal for intermediate correctness. Recent advances such as Decoupled Advantage Policy Optimization (DAPO), Generalized Simple Preference Optimization (GSPO), and Generalized Direct Preference Optimization (GDPO) refine the framework by introducing stabilized clipping, sequence-level policy ratios, and decoupled multi-reward normalization to enhance sample efficiency.

## Reweighting Approaches

SERL introduces a reinforcement learning framework for multi-turn LLM agents that uses environment-conditioned teacher signals to selectively reweight GRPO updates based on hindsight feedback.

## Challenges with Outcome-Based Rewards

Training becomes increasingly dominated by incorrect rollouts, and many such rollouts contain substantial portions of correct reasoning, yet outcome-based RL treats these correct steps the same as the critical mistakes that cause failure.

## Alternative Approaches

TEMPO converts answer groups for one prompt into a prefix tree and computes nonparametric prefix values by averaging descendant outcomes, using branch-gated TD corrections to assign credit at branches. Additionally, HICRA (Hierarchy-aware Credit Assignment) focuses optimization pressure directly on emergent strategic bottlenecks by selectively amplifying the learning signal for planning tokens, accelerating the exploration and reinforcement of effective high-level reasoning.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about ThinkPRM:

## Overview

ThinkPRM is a long CoT verifier fine-tuned on orders of magnitude fewer process labels than those required by discriminative PRMs. ThinkPRM is a collection of generative long CoT process reward models obtained by finetuning reasoning models over 1K synthetic verification CoTs—filtered based on only 8K process labels from PRM800K.

## Generative vs. Discriminative Approach

Generative PRMs frame verification as a language-generation task, producing correctness decisions as natural language tokens accompanied by verification chain-of-thought (CoT). This contrasts with discriminative PRMs which function as classifiers that predict numerical correctness scores for each reasoning step, requiring extensive step-level annotations.

## Performance Comparisons

The resulting verifiers outperform LLM-as-a-judge, discriminative PRMs, on most in- and out-of-domain setups. More specifically, on a subset of GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench, ThinkPRM surpasses discriminative verifiers trained on full PRM800K by 8% and 4.5%, respectively.

## Available Models

ThinkPRM trained PRMs are released in two sizes: 1.5B and 14B finetuned from R1-Distill-Qwen models, with a 7B version added in May 2025 based on Deepseek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.

Based on the search results, I found detailed information about SRaR (Step-wise Rubric Rewards) and related research:

## SRaR (Step-wise Rubric Rewards)

SRaR is an RLVR framework that uses an LLM judge to attribute each rubric item to a specific reasoning step and normalizes per-step rubric scores. 

### Evidence of Improvement Over RaR

Step-attributed judging with per-step token assignment raises the Faithful Reasoning Rate from 34.5% to 46.7%. Additionally, the resulting step-level credit assignment reduces self-correction looping from 48.1% to 26.5%. With Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct as the judge, SRaR achieves a +1.90 average improvement over RaR.

### Structured Reward Performance

The best RaR variant achieves relative improvements of up to 31% on HealthBench and 7% on GPQA-Diamond over popular LLM-as-judge baselines that rely on direct Likert-based rewards. Using rubrics as structured reward signals yields better alignment for smaller judges and reduces performance variance across judge scales.

### Outperforming Binary Methods

The research addresses limitations of binary approaches. Rubric-based methods introduce finer-grained supervision by scoring rollouts against structured criteria, with findings that 18.2% of steps in correct-answer responses are wrong yet positively rewarded, while 49.9% of steps in incorrect-answer responses are correct yet penalized.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about reinforcement learning, credit assignment, and process rewards. Here are the key findings:

## Fine-Grained Credit Assignment and Challenges

Step-level credit assignment is the process of localizing responsibility for observed outcomes back to specific individual steps within a temporal or logical sequence, and underpins efficient learning and robust credit propagation in reinforcement learning, sequential decision-making, and structured reasoning.

However, there are important trade-offs: The absence of granular feedback in outcome-based methods means the model cannot differentiate between partially correct and entirely flawed reasoning, making it difficult to learn robust reasoning logic. At the same time, existing methods providing fine-grained credit are prone to reward hacking, especially when they rely on reward models or other complicated external sources.

## Alternative Approaches

Recent research has explored different credit assignment formulations. The canonical summation-form credit assignment in reinforcement learning easily induces language models to hack steps with high rewards, while min-form credit assignment formulates the value function as the minimum of future rewards.

Additionally, research has shown that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) equipped with an outcome reward model is equivalent to a process reward model-aware objective equipped with a nontrivial, Monte-Carlo-based process reward model.

The search results suggest that while fine-grained credit assignment is theoretically important, the relationship between structured processes and actual incentive structures in RL remains nuanced and actively researched.

## Key Findings on RL Reasoning with Structured Rewards

**Progressive Reward Shaping for Convergence Speed:**
Agentic RL faces challenges from sparse rewards and gradient degradation in Group Relative Policy Optimization, which has been addressed through Progressive Reward Shaping (PRS) and Value-based Sampling Policy Optimization (VSPO). These techniques enable LLM-based reasoning agents to converge faster and generalize better across domains.

**Sample Efficiency Improvements:**
The Cog-Rethinker framework introduces hierarchical metacognitive reinforcement learning with decomposition and reflection rollout stages, achieving better performance while requiring fewer samples. **Systematic Error Suppression:**
Recent approaches shift from mainly encouraging positive responses to actively suppressing negative ones, enabling models to enhance performance while preserving output diversity. However, indiscriminately suppressing negative responses may introduce gradient conflict from semantic overlap between positive and negative distributions.

**Multi-Agent Convergence:**
Potential-based LLM-guided agent-specific reward shaping in multi-agent settings led to drastically reduced convergence steps.

## Overview

MathArena is a benchmark for evaluating large language models on mathematical reasoning using uncontaminated problems from recent human competitions. ## Core Concept

Recurring math competitions produce a rich source of high-quality, uncontaminated problems. These problems are pre-vetted by the competition organizers for originality, ensuring that similar problems have not appeared previously and thereby reducing contamination risk.

Now I have enough research to synthesize and make thoughtful revisions. Let me think deeply about each issue:

## Issue 1: ThinkPRM citation
This is straightforward — ThinkPRM is indeed the most prominent generative PRM and should be cited. Key facts:
- Published April 2025, published in TMLR March 2026
- Generates verification chain-of-thought (free-text reasoning about whether each step is correct)
- Uses only 1% of PRM800K labels (8K process labels or 1K synthetic verification CoTs)
- Outperforms discriminative PRMs on ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME'24, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench


- ThinkPRM-14B achieves 86.5% F1 on ProcessBench

The key distinction here is that ThinkPRM generates free-text verification reasoning about step correctness, whereas DiagPRM focuses on structured misconception diagnosis — this actually validates the generative PRM approach while highlighting the unique gap that DiagPRM addresses.

## Issue 2: RLVR effectiveness debate
The critical tension is in the NeurIPS 2025 oral presentation, which argues that RL primarily improves sampling efficiency rather than fundamental reasoning capability, with base models achieving higher pass@k at large k values.

But I think misconception-specific rewards still provide meaningful benefits even in a reweighting regime. Based on the search results, I found several recent papers (from 2026) that discuss RLVR limitations and the debate about whether it's essentially a reweighting process. Here's what the research shows:

## Key Limitations and Debate

RLVR behaves like a conservative reweighting process, mostly reshaping probability mass within the base model's existing solution space, without adding meaningful mass to new, correct completions that the base model missed.

RL fine-tuning enhances sampling efficiency without expanding the reasoning capacity already present in base models. More specifically, RL-trained variants shine at low sampling budgets, yet base models consistently overtake them as k increases, with RLVR optimizing within, rather than beyond, the base distribution.

## Countering Arguments

However, there is active debate on this question. There is active debate about whether RLVR elicits genuinely novel reasoning or merely reweights reasoning paths already latent in the base model, with conflicting evidence indicating that RLVR can induce capabilities not present in base models. Carefully reshaping the reward function and deploying an enhanced training schedule has shown to be effective in improving exploration during RLVR.

## Why RLVR Remains Valuable

For large reasoning models, recent studies show that replaying successful trajectories accelerates convergence and improves reasoning capabilities. Additionally, the Gradient Gap formalizes the direction of improvement from low-reward to high-reward regions of the response space, with convergence critically depending on aligning the update direction with this Gradient Gap.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about CAPO and related concepts:

## CAPO: Credit Assignment Policy Optimization

CAPO (Credit Assignment Policy Optimization) is a method introduced to address challenges in LLM reasoning. It is an efficient and simple method that improves LLM reasoning by utilizing an LLM as a Generative Process Reward Model (LLM-as-GenPRM) to provide verifiable and fine-grained credit assignment.

### Key Features

Inspired by GRPO's simplicity, CAPO discards the probabilistic value estimation of process rewards and adopts a deterministic, binary evaluation. The approach focuses solely on the intrinsic correctness of each step—identifying objective errors like flawed calculations or logic—rather than predicting its long-term value.

### Technical Approach

CAPO directly leverages an off-the-shelf, general-purpose LLM as a Generative Process Reward Model to generate all step-wise critique by one pass, thereby providing verifiable token-level rewards to refine the tokens that were originally assigned identical rule-based rewards. To enhance the accuracy and robustness of CAPO, voting mechanisms that scale with the number of generated critiques are employed.

### Problem It Solves

Current RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) methods typically treat whole responses as single actions, assigning the same reward to every token. This coarse-grained feedback hampers precise credit assignment, making it hard for models to identify which reasoning steps lead to success or failure.

The paper appears to have been released in October 2025 and is available on arXiv and OpenReview.

## Background
The research idea is "DiagPRM" — a misconception-grounded generative process reward model for mathematical reasoning that produces structured JSON triplets (error mechanism + misconception hypothesis + counterfactual correction). It's been through 4 rounds of review with stagnation (scores ~3.5 across rounds).

## Three Issues from Round 4 Review

### Issue 1: Missing ThinkPRM Citation (2504.16828)
ThinkPRM (TMLR March 2026) is the most prominent generative PRM. It generates free-text verification chain-of-thought reasoning about whether each step is correct. Uses only 1% of PRM800K labels. Outperforms discriminative PRMs: +8% on GPQA-Diamond, +4.5% on LiveCodeBench, 86.5% F1 on ProcessBench with 14B model. 7.2% better than LLM-as-Judge on ProcessBench.

Differentiation from DiagPRM: ThinkPRM generates free-text verification CoT ("is this step correct?") — it reasons about correctness but does not produce structured misconception diagnoses, misconception labels from a grounded taxonomy, or enable cross-problem gradient transfer. DiagPRM generates structured JSON triplets ("why is this step wrong?") with taxonomy-grounded misconception hypotheses. ThinkPRM validates the generative PRM paradigm while leaving the misconception-diagnosis gap open.

### Issue 2: RLVR Effectiveness Debate (CRITICAL)
NeurIPS 2025 oral paper (2504.13837) "Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?" shows:
- RL primarily improves sampling efficiency (pass@1) not fundamental reasoning boundaries (pass@large_k)
- All reasoning paths in RLVR models already exist in base model
- Six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and "remain far from optimal"
- Active debate continues — some evidence RLVR can induce capabilities under certain conditions
- "The Invisible Leash" (2507.14843) confirms RLVR is "support-constrained optimization" — narrows rather than broadens solution space

Key arguments for why misconception-specific rewards still help in the reweighting regime:
(a) Even if RL only reweights, targeted reweighting > uniform reweighting. Binary rewards treat all errors equally; misconception-specific penalties differentially suppress systematic errors.

(e) Practical deployment uses pass@1 or small k — even if ceiling is same, faster convergence to correct paths has enormous value.
(f) Should add convergence speed (RL steps to reach X% accuracy) as explicit evaluation metric alongside final accuracy.

### Issue 3: AIME 2024 Contamination
MathArena (2505.23281) documents:
- 10-20% score inflation on AIME 2024 across most LLMs
- QwQ-Preview-32B shows extreme ~60% inflation
- AIME 2025 scores align with human expectations (uncontaminated)

Fine-tuned on orders of magnitude fewer process labels than discriminative PRMs — uses only 8K process labels or 1K synthetic verification CoTs (1% of PRM800K). ThinkPRM-14B achieves 86.5% F1 on ProcessBench, +8% over discriminative PRMs on GPQA-Diamond, +4.5% on LiveCodeBench, and 7.2% better than LLM-as-Judge on ProcessBench. Key precedent: validates that generative reasoning about correctness outperforms discriminative scoring, and that specialized verification CoT is more effective than generic LLM judgment. **Critical differences from our work**: (a) generates free-text verification CoT ('is this step correct?') vs. our structured JSON triplets with taxonomy-grounded misconception labels ('why is this step wrong?'); (b) no misconception hypothesis — identifies WHETHER a step is wrong but not the underlying cognitive misunderstanding that caused it; (c) unstructured natural language output vs. machine-parseable structured triplets enabling programmatic downstream use; (d) no misconception taxonomy grounding or cross-problem transfer mechanism — ThinkPRM's free-text output lacks the structured labels needed to identify shared misconceptions across different problems; (e) designed for test-time verification (best-of-N, reward-guided search) rather than structured RL training signal generation with misconception-specific penalties. ThinkPRM validates the paradigm DiagPRM extends: from verification to diagnosis.

**RLVR effectiveness debate — 'Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity?' (2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 oral) and 'The Invisible Leash' (2507.14843):** The NeurIPS 2025 oral demonstrates that RL primarily improves sampling efficiency (pass@1) rather than expanding fundamental reasoning boundaries (pass@large_k) — all reasoning paths in RLVR models already exist in the base model. Six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and 'remain far from optimal.' The Invisible Leash confirms RLVR is 'support-constrained optimization' — the shrinkage of empirical support generally outweighs expansion, narrowing rather than broadening the solution space. **Implications for DiagPRM**: This reweighting interpretation does not invalidate structured reward signals — it reframes their benefit. Within the reweighting regime, the question shifts from 'can RL discover new reasoning?' to 'can RL efficiently allocate probability mass to correct existing paths?' Empirically, SRaR (+3.57), Data-Driven Rubrics (+45%), and CAPO demonstrate that structured/fine-grained rewards outperform binary even within this interpretation. DiagPRM's misconception-specific rewards extend this further via cross-problem gradient transfer (see RL integration below).

**Evaluation contamination — MathArena (2505.23281):** Documents strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024, with 10-20% score inflation across most LLMs and QwQ-Preview-32B showing extreme ~60% inflation. AIME 2025 scores align with human expectations (uncontaminated). MathArena evaluates 50+ models across seven competitions (162 total problems) using newly released competitions to eliminate contamination risk. Motivates our replacement of AIME 2024 with AIME 2025/2026 in evaluation.

Math rubrics contain ~250 items across 169 keywords. Achieves +45% accuracy over general LLM-as-judge, approaches supervised reward model performance with 20% as many gold labels. This is the closest existing work to DiagPRM's pipeline (auto-discover error patterns → structured reward → RL). **Critical differences**: (a) Rubrics capture error TYPE — descriptive classification of WHAT went wrong (e.g., 'incorrect algebraic manipulation') — while DiagPRM provides causal misconception HYPOTHESES explaining WHY the error occurred (e.g., 'EXPONENT_DISTRIBUTES_OVER_ADDITION: student applied (a+b)^n = a^n + b^n'), enabling fundamentally different downstream use; (b) binary reward output (error present/absent → 0/1) vs. our structured JSON triplets (mechanism + misconception + correction) providing continuous, multi-dimensional reward signals; (c) per-problem rubric application with no cross-problem transfer mechanism vs. our shared misconception penalties enabling gradient transfer across all problems exhibiting the same misconception; (d) admitted specificity limitation (≤0.662 even on training data) vs. our symbolic verification + cross-model consensus achieving higher-fidelity diagnosis; (e) no counterfactual correction component.
